metadata.title: Does between-school tracking really result in more achievement homogeneous schools? Evidence from 40 countries around the globe
metadata.venue: Research in Social Stratification and Mobility

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses individual student data from TIMSS 2011 (Grade 4), PIRLS 2011 (Grade 4), and PISA 2018 (age 15) and applies a two-level multilevel framework where schools are the Level 2 units. In the Stage 1 multilevel analyses, the authors explicitly state that school weights are used as Level 2 weights and that no weight is used at Level 1, following Mang et al. (2021) for educational large-scale assessments. This indicates that complex survey design features are incorporated through school-level weighting rather than through student-level weighting. For Stage 2, the country-level effect sizes (differences in standardized within- and between-school variance components) are meta-analyzed using random-effects models with inverse-variance weighting, and the authors note that this weighting can affect small deviations from simple intercept-based averages.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper states that achievement scores used to compute WSAV and BSAV are based on plausible values, but it does not report the specific plausible-value combining rule (e.g., Rubin’s rules) or the exact missing-data strategy for the retained variables. Given that large-scale assessment datasets typically contain missingness in background variables and/or item responses, the absence of a documented missing-data handling approach is a reporting gap that limits reproducibility of the variance-component estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample includes only countries that participated in either (PIRLS 2011 + PISA 2018) or (TIMSS 2011 + PISA 2018), yielding 40 countries total. For comparability, subnational participation was matched across assessments (e.g., only Alberta/Ontario/Quebec for Canada; only England and Northern Ireland for the UK; only Flemish Belgium for PISA–TIMSS and only French Belgium for PISA–PIRLS). Countries were further restricted to those with PISA population coverage of at least 80% (Coverage Index 3), excluding Bulgaria, Colombia, Morocco, Romania, Thailand, and Turkey from the main analyses. Saudi Arabia was excluded because age-of-first-selection data were unavailable. For the multilevel variance decomposition, the retained variables were achievement scores (reading/math/science) used to compute WSAV and BSAV, along with student/school/country IDs and student and school weights; students participating in both PIRLS and TIMSS in the same year were counted once.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2011 Grade 4 Reading and PISA 2018 Reading (age 15) — WSAV/BSAV change
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random-effects meta-analysis (weighted mean effect size): WSAV change in early-tracking countries μ̂ = -15.33 (p < .05); baseline WSAV change across all countries μ̂ = -10.19 (95% CI [-16.96, -3.42]); mixed-effects moderator test: early vs late WSAV change B = 16.74 (p = .055) for reading; tracking explains 5.2% of between-country variation in WSAV change (QM[2] = 5.73, p = .057).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2011 Grade 4 Reading and PISA 2018 Reading the study estimated within-school achievement variation (WSAV) change between age 10 and age 15 and tested moderation by tracking regime (first selection age). It found that WSAV decreased in early-tracking countries (μ̂ = -15.33, p < .05) and that the overall WSAV change was negative (μ̂ = -10.19), but the early-vs-late difference was only marginal (B = 16.74, p = .055). This indicates that between-school tracking produces only small and domain-specific improvements in within-school homogeneity, suggesting policy should not rely on tracking alone to reduce within-school achievement dispersion.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2011 Grade 4 Reading and PISA 2018 Reading (age 15) — WSAV/BSAV change
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random-effects meta-analysis (weighted mean effect size): BSAV change in early-tracking countries μ̂ = 25.64 (p < .05); baseline BSAV change across all countries μ̂ = 10.27 (95% CI [3.37, 17.15]); mixed-effects moderator test: early vs late BSAV change B = -28.50 (p < .05); tracking explains 12.5% of between-country variation in BSAV change (QM[2] = 12.11, p = .002).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2011 Grade 4 Reading and PISA 2018 Reading the study estimated between-school achievement variation (BSAV) change between age 10 and age 15 and tested moderation by tracking regime (first selection age). It found that BSAV increased substantially in early-tracking countries (μ̂ = 25.64, p < .05) and that overall BSAV change was positive (μ̂ = 10.27). The early-vs-late moderation was significant (B = -28.50, p < .05), indicating a much larger BSAV increase under earlier selection. This indicates that tracking tends to widen achievement differences between schools even when within-school homogeneity gains are limited, implying that policymakers should weigh tracking’s sorting effects against its weak homogenization benefits.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2011 Grade 4 Math and PISA 2018 Math (age 15) — WSAV/BSAV change
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random-effects meta-analysis (weighted mean effect size): WSAV change in early-tracking countries μ̂ = -8.73 (p = .198); baseline WSAV change across all countries μ̂ = -7.20 (95% CI [-13.00, -1.41]); mixed-effects moderator test: early vs late WSAV change B = 7.81 (p = .339); tracking explains 0.3% of between-country variation in WSAV change (QM[2] = 2.26, p = .323).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2011 Grade 4 Math and PISA 2018 Math the study estimated within-school achievement variation (WSAV) change between age 10 and age 15 and tested moderation by tracking regime (first selection age). It found that WSAV decreased overall (μ̂ = -7.20, 95% CI [-13.00, -1.41]) but the early-tracking-specific decrease was not statistically significant (μ̂ = -8.73, p = .198). Moreover, early vs late differences were not significant (B = 7.81, p = .339), and tracking explained almost none of the between-country variation in WSAV change (0.3%). This indicates that tracking does not reliably reduce within-school dispersion in mathematics, suggesting that instructional differentiation needs to be strengthened regardless of tracking policy.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2011 Grade 4 Math and PISA 2018 Math (age 15) — WSAV/BSAV change
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random-effects meta-analysis (weighted mean effect size): BSAV change in early-tracking countries μ̂ = 26.50 (p < .05); baseline BSAV change across all countries μ̂ = 7.16 (95% CI [-0.45, 14.76]); mixed-effects moderator test: early vs late BSAV change B = -27.36 (p < .05); tracking explains 8.3% of between-country variation in BSAV change (QM[2] = 8.49, p = .014).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2011 Grade 4 Math and PISA 2018 Math the study estimated between-school achievement variation (BSAV) change between age 10 and age 15 and tested moderation by tracking regime (first selection age). It found that BSAV increased markedly in early-tracking countries (μ̂ = 26.50, p < .05) and that overall BSAV change was positive (μ̂ = 7.16). The moderation by tracking timing was significant (B = -27.36, p < .05), with larger BSAV increases under earlier selection. This indicates that early between-school tracking amplifies between-school inequality in mathematics, implying that equity-focused interventions should target low tracks and school-level resource allocation rather than assuming tracking will homogenize learning.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2011 Grade 4 Science and PISA 2018 Science (age 15) — WSAV/BSAV change
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random-effects meta-analysis (weighted mean effect size): WSAV change in early-tracking countries μ̂ = -7.48 (p = .234); baseline WSAV change across all countries μ̂ = -5.01 (95% CI [-12.46, -2.44]); mixed-effects moderator test: early vs late WSAV change B = 16.05 (p = .102); tracking explains 6.9% of between-country variation in WSAV change (QM[2] = 7.45, p = .024) and is significant in the general model (QM[2] = 15.34, p < .001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2011 Grade 4 Science and PISA 2018 Science the study estimated within-school achievement variation (WSAV) change between age 10 and age 15 and tested moderation by tracking regime (first selection age). It found that WSAV decreased overall (μ̂ = -5.01) but the early-tracking-specific decrease was not significant (μ̂ = -7.48, p = .234). Tracking timing showed a significant moderation for WSAV change in science at the meta-regression level (QM[2] = 7.45, p = .024), though the early-vs-late contrast was not significant (B = 16.05, p = .102). This indicates that any within-school homogenization effect of tracking in science is inconsistent and likely secondary to between-school sorting, implying that policy should prioritize teaching quality and support for heterogeneity.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2011 Grade 4 Science and PISA 2018 Science (age 15) — WSAV/BSAV change
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random-effects meta-analysis (weighted mean effect size): BSAV change in early-tracking countries μ̂ = 29.18 (p < .05); baseline BSAV change across all countries μ̂ = 5.12 (95% CI [-3.40, 13.64]); mixed-effects moderator test: early vs late BSAV change B = -30.60 (p < .05); tracking explains 10.1% of between-country variation in BSAV change (QM[2] = 10.45, p = .005).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2011 Grade 4 Science and PISA 2018 Science the study estimated between-school achievement variation (BSAV) change between age 10 and age 15 and tested moderation by tracking regime (first selection age). It found that BSAV increased strongly in early-tracking countries (μ̂ = 29.18, p < .05) and that overall BSAV change was positive (μ̂ = 5.12). The early-vs-late moderation was significant (B = -30.60, p < .05), indicating larger between-school inequality under earlier selection. This indicates that early between-school tracking increases science achievement stratification between schools, suggesting that reforms should focus on reducing track-based resource and instruction gaps.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses a two-stage individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis combining TIMSS 2011 Grade 4 (math and science), PIRLS 2011 Grade 4 (reading), and PISA 2018 (age 15) across 40 countries (with PISA coverage ≥80%). The authors decompose achievement variance into within-school achievement variation (WSAV) and between-school achievement variation (BSAV) using multilevel variance decomposition, then compute DID-style differences in WSAV/BSAV from Grade 4 to age 15 and synthesize them with random-effects meta-analysis and mixed-effects meta-regressions. Across domains, WSAV reductions are small and statistically significant mainly for reading (early tracking μ̂ = -15.33, p < .05), while BSAV increases are large in early-tracking countries (reading μ̂ = 25.64; math μ̂ = 26.50; science μ̂ = 29.18, all p < .05). Tracking timing significantly moderates BSAV change (e.g., reading QM[2] = 12.11, p = .002), but WSAV moderation is weaker and domain-dependent. Limitations include the absence of a documented missing-data strategy and the fact that this is not ML prediction; causal claims are limited by the pseudo-panel DID assumptions and cross-assessment comparability.
